title: Comparison of deep plasma proteome enrichment methods
projectDescription: Plasma is a complex biological fluid containing extracellular vesicles (EVs), residual platelets, and soluble proteins, all of which can serve as biomarkers for pathological conditions. While conventional plasma proteomics typically identifies hundreds of proteins, recent enrichment strategies have expanded coverage to thousands. It is not clear yet whether   these methods enrich preferentially different classes of protein and whether they allow for reliable quantification Here, we compared three common advanced proteomic workflows—Seer Proteograph (nanoparticle-based), MagNET (SCX magnetic beads), and ENRICHplus (PreOmics)—as well as EV enrichment obtained by centrifugation. We aimed to explore the content in soluble proteins, EV cargo, and platelet-derived proteins in platelet-poor plasma (PPP) from healthy donors after the enrichments. Samples were analyzed using timsTOF platforms and quantified with DIA-NN in library-free mode. Functional insights were obtained using Over-Representation Analysis (ORA), Human Protein Atlas annotations, and EV-specific markers. Quantification was evaluated comparing each method to neat plasma using protein coefficient of variation and point-biserial correlation. We quantified an average of ~4500 proteins with EV centrifugation, ~4000 with Seer, ~2800 with ENRICHplus, ~2300 with MagNET, and ~900 with neat plasma. Each method enriched distinct protein signatures: EV markers such as CD81 were predominantly detected in EV preparations; lipoproteins were enriched in ENRICHplus; cytokine and hormone signaling pathways were most evident in Seer. Platelet protein intensity was directly correlated with total protein identifications but did not compromise quantification of low-abundance proteins. Across 50 healthy individuals, Proteograph consistently demonstrated reproducible enrichment and depletion patterns, with notable exceptions for proteins such as FCN3, F11, and FCGBP.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Plasma Collection and Preparation: Peripheral blood was collected from eight healthy volunteers, three of which delivered by the French Blood Establishment in EDTA tubes. The three enrichment methods as well as EV centrifugation have been performed using plasma from healthy volunteers and prepared in our laboratory. A cohort of fifty health individuals was used for comparing Proteograph with neat plasma analysis. Informed consent was obtained from all healthy volunteers. Peripheral blood was collected in EDTA tubes and plasma (2 mL) was obtained by centrifuging the blood twice at 1,500 g for 10 min. All samples were immediately stored at –80°C.  Platelet isolation: Briefly, peripheral blood was centrifuged at 200 g for 10 min and the supernatant was retained for subsequent processing. To prevent contamination of the platelet-rich plasma fraction with erythrocytes, the bottom 500 µL of plasma was discarded. The sample was then centrifuged again at 200 g for 10 min. This process was repeated once more, and after centrifugation at 2,000 g for 15 minutes, the supernatant and platelets were collected. The platelets were washed twice by adding 4 mL of PBS containing 1.6 mg/mL EDTA, followed by centrifugation at 2,000 g for 15 min. After discarding the supernatant, the purified platelet fraction was collected. EV preparation: Centrifugation method: Extracellular vesicles were isolated by a centrifugation method based on the protocol published by Geiger’s laboratory. All the steps were carried out at 4°C. Briefly, plasma was prepared from peripheral blood and centrifuged at 3,300 g for 20 min. Supernatants were collected in clean tubes, diluted 2-fold with ice-cold PBS and centrifuged at 20,000 g for 1 h. Pelleted extracellular vesicles were then washed twice with the same volume of ice-cold PBS and suspended in 5% SDS, 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate. Mag-Net enrichment: EV preparation was carried out using MagReSyn strong anion exchange beads according to the manufacturers’ protocol. Automated steps for Mag-Net enrichment, extraction, digestion, and Evotip loading were carried out on 20 µL of plasma samples using the Opentrons OT-2 robotic liquid handling platform and their established protocol. Briefly, plasma were incubated with the magnetic beads for 20 min. Then, samples were washed for 10 min and digested onto the beads with trypsin for 4 h at room temparature . Peptides were then directly loaded onto Evotips with the OT-2 and analysed by LC-MS/MS. PreOmics ENRICHplus: Plasma samples (50µl) were processed using the ENRICHplus kit following the manufacturer's instructions. Samples were dried down in a SpeedVac and peptides were resuspended in 15µL of 2% ACN, 0.1 %FA. Peptide concentration was determined by Nanodrop and 200ng were injected into the LC-MS/MS. Seer Proteograph XT: Plasma samples (250µl) were prepared using the Proteograph XT kit following the manufacturer's instructions. Peptide quantification was performed using the Pierce Quantitative Fluorometric Peptide Assay. The samples were dried in a SpeedVac and reconstituted at a concentration of 50ng/µL. After reconstitution, peptides from NPA and NPB were pooled and a total of 600ng of peptides was injected into the LC-MS/MS. Protein digestion: S-TrapTM micro spin column digestion was performed on 1µL of neat plasma, on EV and platelets pellets  according to manufacturer’s instructions.  Peptides were resuspended in 2% ACN, 0.1% formic acid in HPLC-grade water and 400ng were injected on an Evosep One system coupled to a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer. The Evosep One system operated with the Whisper Zoom 40 Samples Per Day or 30 Samples Per Day method (for Mag-Net samples) using a 15 cm C18 Aurora Elite column and a 15 cm Performance column respectively. Mass-spectrometric data were acquired using the parallel accumulation serial fragmentation acquisition method in DIA mode with a 19-windows method using 33 Da windows covering the mobility ranges over a 400-1050 m/z range.
dataProcessingProtocol: Data analysis of all DIA files was performed using DIA-NN software [17] (version 1.8.1). A search against the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens database (downloaded either in January 2024, 20428 entries or in July 2024, 20435 entries) was performed using library free workflow. For this purpose, “FASTA digest for library free search/library generation” and “Deep learning spectra, RTs and IMs prediction” options were checked for precursor ion generation. A maximum of 1 trypsin missed cleavages was allowed and the maximum variable modification was set to 2. Carbamidomethylation (Cys) was set as the fixed modification, whereas protein N-terminal methionine excision, methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation were set as variable modifications. The peptide length range was set to 7–30 amino acids, precursor charge range 2–4, precursor m/z range 300–1300, and fragment ion m/z range 300–1300. To search the parent mass and fragment ions, accuracy was set to 10 ppm manually. The false discovery rates (FDRs) at the protein and peptide level were set to 1%. Match between runs was allowed.  All subsequent differential analysis was performed with Mass Dynamics 2.0 [18]. In brief, all protein intensities were log2 transformed to perform statistics. Data were then filtered to keep only proteins with 50% valid values in at least one group. Afterward, data were imputed to fill missing data points by creating a Gaussian distribution of random numbers with a standard deviation of 30% relative to the standard deviation of the measured values and 1.8 standard deviation downshift of the mean to simulate the distribution of low signal values. Finally, statistical analysis was performed at a FDR of 5% after Benjamini Hochberg correction.   All R figures was created using R (version 4.4) and RStudio (version 2024.12). The majority of the figures were created using ggplot2 (v3.5.1) embedded in the tidyverse [19] (v2.0) . In particular for Principal Component Analysis and Interactive Heatmap, the PCAtools (v2.18.0) and the InteractiveComplexHeatmap [20] (v1.14.0) R packages were used, respectively. To draw paired plot and Upset plot, ggpubr (v0.6) and UpSetR (v1.4.0) R packages were used, respectively. Over Representation Analysis using Cellular Component Gene Ontology (GO CC) and subsequent representation of the results was performed using genekitr [21] (v1.2.8) with following parameters (geneset = hg_gs, padj_method = "BH", p_cutoff = 0.05, q_cutoff = 0.05, min_gset_size = 10, max_gset_size = 500). In particular for the ORA of the identified heatmap clusters, the clusterProfiler [22] (v4.14.4) and enrichplot (v 1.27.4) R packages were used, respectively. To allow parallel enrichment analysis of different gene list from different heatmap clusters, the compareCluster() function was used with the following parameters (fun = enrichGO,  ont = "ALL",  OrgDb ="org.Hs.eg.db", pAdjustMethod = "BH", keyType = "SYMBOL", pvalueCutoff  = 0.05, qvalueCutoff  = 0.05, minGSSize = 10, maxGSSize = 500) and using the genome wide annoatation for Human org.Hs.eg.db (v3.20.0). For particular analysis, Human Protein Atlas (v24.0) (Human Protein Atlas proteinatlas.org) was used and more specifically the HPA IHC data (“normal_ihc_data.tsv”, downloaded in December 2024) and the global protein atlas database (proteinatlas.tsv downloaded in November 2024) were used to retrieve knowledge-based information from our dataset. Plasma contamination list was downloaded from the Quality Control of the Plasma Proteome [14]  Mannlabs github (https://github.com/MannLabs/Quality-Control-of-the-Plasma-Proteome/tree/master/data). To evaluate the quantitative performance of three enrichment techniques, we compared protein quantification profiles before and after enrichment. Two parameters were calculated for each protein across biological replicates: (i) the ratio of coefficient of variation (CV) after enrichment relative to the CV in neat plasma (ratio = CVenrich(%)/CVneat(%) when ratio ≥ 1 and the negative reciprocal - CVneat(%)/CVenrich(%) when 0 < ratio < 1), and (ii) the point-biserial correlation coefficient (rpb), which quantifies the degree and the consistency of depletion or enrichment. All R codes are provided as a supplementary material for transparency and reproducibility.
